title: CK Vulpeculae seen with Gemini North
caption: The CK Vulpeculae nebula, imaged by the Gemini North telescope
credit: International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA. Image processing: Travis Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage), Jen Miller (Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab), Mahdi Zamani & Davide de Martin

recognition.text: Official NSF NOIRLab / Gemini press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This Gemini North image shows the enigmatic CK Vulpeculae nebula. Two small reddish arcs, one about a quarter of the way up from the bottom and another about a quarter of the way down from the top, turned out to be key to understanding it.

A team of astronomers measured how fast those arcs are moving and how their positions have shifted over time. Their results helped show that the nebula is growing five times faster than astronomers had previously thought.

Comparing how fast something moves toward or away from us with how far it seems to drift across the sky over the years can help astronomers pin down its distance and the scale of the event that launched it. The picture was taken with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph through filters for oxygen, sulfur and hydrogen-alpha, each isolating the light of one kind of glowing gas.

understand.summary: Taken in visible light with GMOS on Gemini North through [O III], S II and hydrogen-alpha filters; the colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Narrow filters isolate the glow of particular gases, and the long exposure gathers far more light than the eye.
